questions.q: According to this lesson, what does running Airflow self-hosted in production actually commit a team to?
options: A one-time setup with no further maintenance ever required
Owning the metadata database, scheduler/webserver uptime, version upgrades, and worker scaling — all as ongoing operational work
Only writing DAGs, with infrastructure handled automatically
Nothing extra — self-hosted Airflow requires no more upkeep than a local install used for learning
questions.explain: Self-hosting means owning the database, process uptime, upgrades, and scaling as real, ongoing operational responsibilities.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three managed Airflow options this lesson names?
options: Jenkins
Microsoft Power Automate
Kubernetes CronJobs
AWS MWAA (Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow)
questions.explain: The three named managed options are Astronomer, AWS MWAA, and Google Cloud Composer.

questions.q: When using a managed Airflow option instead of self-hosting, what stays the same?
options: DAGs work completely differently on managed platforms
You still write the same DAGs, operators, and connections taught throughout this course
You no longer need to write any Python code at all
Operators are replaced by a drag-and-drop interface
questions.explain: Managed options change who runs the underlying infrastructure — the DAG-writing itself is the same Airflow you've learned throughout this course.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real tradeoff between self-hosted and managed Airflow?
options: Self-hosted is always objectively better in every situation
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
Operational burden vs. cost vs. control — they move together, and there's no single 'best' option
Managed options are always cheaper in raw dollar terms
questions.explain: Self-hosting gives more control at lower direct cost but higher operational burden; managed options cost more but shift that burden to the vendor.

questions.q: Why might a small team with no dedicated infrastructure engineers prefer a managed option, even at higher dollar cost?
options: Managed options remove the need to write any DAGs
The real cost of self-hosting without staff to run it is outages nobody's watching for
Self-hosted Airflow cannot run any DAGs with fewer than five engineers
Managed options are always free for small teams
questions.explain: Without staff dedicated to operating the platform, the hidden cost of self-hosting is unmonitored failures — managed options shift that operational responsibility to the vendor.
